title: Draft: ws_hash_func: Add a replacement for g_str_hash() using xxhash.

notes.body: Could some one profile this and see if it's worth it?
Isn't this all the same as `wmem_str_hash` already? I guess maybe there's a reason to move the hash functions into a separate include.
In content yes, I never checked if it would serve as a direct replacement to g_str_hash()
I guess the fallback without XXH is different in the two cases.

added 3 commits
  • 2c8c4daf...e154f0f8 - 2 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • aa3b6547 - ws_hash_func: Add a replacement for g_str_hash() using xxhash.
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20546/diffs?diff_id=1423262581&start_sha=2c8c4daf8d73f2a7050365b2b42b46226ba948b3)

g_str_hash() is a Bernstein/djb2 hash. It generally performs well in 32-bit hash tables not because it has a very small number of collisions or is objectively great in that sense (for large files), but because it's really small which leads to fitting in the CPU instruction cache. At least a decade ago, the recommendation was just to use something like it rather than ostensibly better or more optimal hashes, because the caching made up for everything else when used a bunch in a hash table. (https://rurban.github.io/smhasher/#summary https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/2850583.2850585 https://15721.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2024/papers/09-hashjoins/richter-vldb2015.pdf)

XXH is very fast, though, and well-optimized. Interestingly, doing the XXH3 algorithm that is available starting in 0.8.0 (which has been out since July 2020 and is present in old Linux distributions like RHEL 8 and Debian Bullseye) and just taking the lower 32-bits turns out to be faster than XXH32; certainly on a 64-bit platform, and there are [claims](https://fastcompression.blogspot.com/2019/03/presenting-xxh3.html) that this is true on 32-bits as well.

Here's some cachegrind results on Fedora on a AMD Ryzen 5 5600X. I swapped out g_str_hash() to wmem_str_hash() on proto_names, proto_short_names, proto_filter_names, and gpa_name_map, four of the largest tables. This is just running tshark on test/captures/empty.pcap (with `-n` and also generally without other preferences that would slow things down, like a custom services table or a IEEE 802.11 key that would cause startup of gcrypt.)

Here's some additional results with another commit in my local tree where I expanded the wmem_map implementation to cache the entire calculated hash, which speeds up collisions (and table doublings). (It does add space, and is useless with a g_direct_hash - possibly ideal is to have two implementations, using the smaller version with g_direct_hash.) This should only affect the wmem_map, `gpa_name_map`, which is largest table.

However, running perf demonstrates that while the instructions are a lot better with xxHash, the instructions per cycle are worse, so the gain isn't really what's implied by that. It is faster, but not 10% faster. That's also with gcc. I will try clang as well.

The results might be different with other setups.
Maybe replacing those tables with wmem_map and preset size rather than changing only the hash function is a better strategy.
Missing a semicolon here causes the build failure on platforms without XXHASH.

So changing the wmem_strong_hash() xxhash verion to use XXH3_64bits_withSeed() and use wmem_str_hash() instead of g_str_hsh()

would be the prefered solution? But the actual gain is minor?

Yes, I think so. The claim is that's superior even on a 32-bit system, though I haven't tested. The gain in number of CPU instructions is pretty significant, but the gain in actual execution time in my profiling seems minor (but probably worth it.)

Using your approach with `ws_str_hash` might be preferable to handle cases where HAVE_XXHASH isn't true - we'd fall back to the faster glib djb implementation instead of the slower existing wmem_strong_hash implementation.

I'm not entirely certain that we need a "strong" hash for the hash table. If there's lots of collisions, that impacts performance, but it's not like it's a security issue. (And with a hash table, more collisions but a faster hash can still end up being worth it on performance.)

Maybe fixing up wmem str hash and use it in place of g string hash is even
better.

+#include "config.h"
+
+#include <glib.h>
+#ifdef HAVE_XXHASH
+#include <xxhash.h>
+#endif /* HAVE_XXHASH */
+#include "ws_hash_func.h"
+
+guint
+ws_str_hash(gconstpointer v)
+{
+#ifdef HAVE_XXHASH
+    return (uint32_t)XXH32((const uint8_t*)v, strlen((const char*)v), 0);
+#else
+    g_str_hash(v)
+#endif
+}
